summary.text: Counting multiples of each power of \(p\) and using the factorial valuation formula reduces the numerator and denominator valuations to \(\sum_{e\ge1}\lfloor n/p^e\rfloor^2\) and \(\sum_{e\ge1}\sum_{k=1}^n k\lfloor\lfloor n/p^e\rfloor/k\rfloor\), respectively.  The inner sum is at most \(x^2\), is strictly smaller when \(x\ge3\), and equals \(x^2\) when \(x\le2\); hence the quotient has positive \(p\)-adic valuation exactly when \(\lfloor n/p\rfloor\ge3\), equivalently \(p\le\lfloor n/3\rfloor\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N_n=\prod_{j=1}^n\prod_{k=1}^n \gcd(j,k),
\qquad
D_n=\prod_{k=1}^n\left(\left\lfloor\frac nk\right\rfloor!\right)^k,
\]
and let
\[
a(n)=\frac{N_n}{D_n}.
\]
Initially this quotient may be interpreted as integer division; below we prove that \(D_n\mid N_n\), so it is the ordinary integer ratio appearing in the sequence.

Fix a prime \(p\), and write \(v_p(r)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(r\). All factors in \(N_n\) and \(D_n\) are positive, so the usual rules
\[
v_p(rs)=v_p(r)+v_p(s),\qquad v_p(r^t)=t\,v_p(r)
\]
apply throughout.

We first compute the valuations of the numerator and denominator.

For any positive integer \(r\le n\),
\[
v_p(r)=\sum_{e=1}^n \mathbf 1_{p^e\mid r}.
\]
Indeed, \(p^e\mid r\) holds precisely for \(1\le e\le v_p(r)\). There are exactly \(v_p(r)\) such exponents. The upper limit \(n\) is harmless: since \(p\ge2\), one has \(v_p(r)\le r\le n\). Consequently, for \(1\le j,k\le n\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(\gcd(j,k))
 &=\sum_{e=1}^n \mathbf 1_{p^e\mid\gcd(j,k)}\\
 &=\sum_{e=1}^n \mathbf 1_{p^e\mid j\ \text{and}\ p^e\mid k}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Summing over all ordered pairs \((j,k)\) and interchanging the finite sums gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(N_n)
 &=\sum_{e=1}^n
   \#\{j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:p^e\mid j\}
   \#\{k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:p^e\mid k\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The multiples of a positive integer \(d\) in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) are
\(d,2d,\ldots,\lfloor n/d\rfloor d\), so their number is \(\lfloor n/d\rfloor\). Taking \(d=p^e\), we obtain
\[
\boxed{
 v_p(N_n)=\sum_{e=1}^n\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^e}\right\rfloor^2.}
\tag{1}
\]

For the denominator, Legendre's formula says that for every nonnegative integer \(m\),
\[
v_p(m!)=\sum_{e\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^e}\right\rfloor.
\]
When \(m\le n\), all terms with \(e>n\) vanish, so we may sum from \(1\) to \(n\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(D_n)
 &=\sum_{k=1}^n k\,v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac nk\right\rfloor!\right)\\
 &=\sum_{k=1}^n k\sum_{e=1}^n
   \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor n/k\rfloor}{p^e}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
For positive integers \(k,q\), successive integer divisions satisfy
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor n/k\rfloor}{q}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{n}{kq}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor n/q\rfloor}{k}\right\rfloor.
\]
Using this with \(q=p^e\), and interchanging the two finite sums, gives
\[
\boxed{
 v_p(D_n)=\sum_{e=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^n
 k\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor n/p^e\rfloor}{k}\right\rfloor.}
\tag{2}
\]

We now analyze the inner sum in (2). For nonnegative integers \(x,n\), define
\[
S_n(x)=\sum_{k=1}^n k\left\lfloor\frac{x}{k}\right\rfloor.
\]
In our application \(x=\lfloor n/p^e\rfloor\), and hence \(x\le n\).

First,
\[
S_n(x)\le x^2.
\tag{3}
\]
Indeed, terms with \(k>x\) vanish. For every \(1\le k\le x\),
\[
k\left\lfloor\frac{x}{k}\right\rfloor\le x.
\]
There are at most \(x\) nonzero terms, so their sum is at most \(x\cdot x=x^2\).

If additionally \(x\le n\) and \(x\ge3\), this inequality is strict:
\[
S_n(x)<x^2.
\tag{4}
\]
To see this, all of the terms indexed by \(1\le k\le x\) are at most \(x\), as above, but the term with \(k=x-1\) is strictly smaller. Since \(x\ge3\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{x}{x-1}\right\rfloor=1,
\]
so that term equals \(x-1<x\). Thus the sum of the \(x\) potentially nonzero terms is strictly less than \(x^2\).

At the other extreme, if \(x\le2\) and \(x\le n\), then
\[
S_n(x)=x^2.
\tag{5}
\]
This follows directly from the three cases. If \(x=0\), every term is zero. If \(x=1\), only \(k=1\) contributes, giving \(1\). If \(x=2\), the terms \(k=1,2\) are respectively \(2\) and \(2\), giving \(4\). Terms with \(k>x\) again vanish.

Combining (1), (2), and (3), for every prime \(p\) we have
\[
v_p(D_n)\le v_p(N_n).
\tag{6}
\]
Both numbers are positive. By unique prime factorization, comparison (6) for every prime implies
\[
D_n\mid N_n.
\]
Thus \(a(n)=N_n/D_n\) is a positive integer. Moreover,
\[
N_n=D_n\,a(n),
\]
and hence for every prime \(p\),
\[
v_p(N_n)=v_p(D_n)+v_p(a(n)).
\tag{7}
\]
It follows that
\[
p\mid a(n)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
v_p(a(n))\ge1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
v_p(D_n)<v_p(N_n).
\tag{8}
\]
So it remains only to determine exactly when the inequality in (6) is strict.

Assume first that
\[
p\le\left\lfloor\frac n3\right\rfloor.
\]
Then \(3p\le n\), and therefore
\[
\left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor\ge3.
\]
In the summands corresponding to \(e=1\), put
\(x=\lfloor n/p\rfloor\). Since also \(x\le n\), (4) yields
\[
S_n\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor\right)
<\left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor^2.
\]
For every other exponent \(e\), (3) gives
\[
S_n\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^e}\right\rfloor\right)
\le\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^e}\right\rfloor^2.
\]
Thus, after summing over \(e=1,\ldots,n\), at least one term is strictly smaller and none is larger. Equations (1) and (2) therefore give
\[
v_p(D_n)<v_p(N_n).
\]
By (8), \(p\mid a(n)\).

Conversely, assume
\[
p>\left\lfloor\frac n3\right\rfloor.
\]
We claim that
\[
\left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor\le2.
\]
Otherwise \(\lfloor n/p\rfloor\ge3\), which would imply \(3p\le n\), and hence \(p\le\lfloor n/3\rfloor\), a contradiction. For every \(e\ge1\), we have \(p^e\ge p\), so
\[
0\le\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^e}\right\rfloor
\le\left\lfloor\frac np\right\rfloor\le2.
\]
Also \(\lfloor n/p^e\rfloor\le n\). Formula (5), applied separately to every exponent \(e\), now gives
\[
S_n\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^e}\right\rfloor\right)
=
\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^e}\right\rfloor^2.
\]
Summing and using (1) and (2), we conclude that
\[
v_p(D_n)=v_p(N_n).
\]
By (8), \(p\nmid a(n)\).

We have proved, for every positive integer \(n\) and every prime \(p\),
\[
\boxed{
 p\mid a(n)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 p\le\left\lfloor\frac n3\right\rfloor.}
\]
